A1.justification: Both PDFs describe RIGBD despite the revised title. Their complete main texts, equations, figures, tables, and appendices support comparison, including matching material moved or renumbered in v2.

before.justification: v1 reports original defense, poisoned-node detection, runtime, ablation, and sensitivity experiments on Cora, PubMed, and OGB-arxiv.

after.justification: v2 retains these original experiments and adds results on further datasets, low-degree nodes, heterophilic graphs, and single-node triggers.

M1.justification: Equations 1–6 and Algorithm 1 retain the same random-dropping, prediction-variance detection, threshold selection, and robust-training procedure. Section 4.1 newly documents restoring neighbors when all are dropped; the PDFs do not establish this implementation detail as a change to the earlier method.

E1.justification: Coverage expands from three citation networks to include Citeseer, the Physics coauthorship graph, and the Flickr image graph. Appendices F and K additionally evaluate Wisconsin, Cornell, and Texas, substantially extending coverage to heterophilic graphs while retaining node classification.

E2.justification: The corresponding comparisons retain GCN, GNNGuard, RobustGCN, Prune, OD, RS, and ABL, with the same additional GAT, GraphSage, and RS configurations. GTA, UGBA, and DPGBA remain the evaluated attacks; newly cited attacks are not added as evaluated comparators.

E3.justification: New protocols include degree-1/2/3 comparisons using UGBA with K=10 and a 0.5 drop ratio, heterophilic defense tests with 20 poisoned training nodes, and single-node-trigger tests. The retained experiments preserve their splits, metrics, backbone configurations, and principal settings.

E4.justification: New Appendices F, K, and P investigate whether low-degree clean nodes confound detection, whether defense remains effective on heterophilic graphs, and whether smaller triggers evade defense. These substantially extend robustness analysis beyond the retained component ablations, dropping-parameter sensitivity, and poisoning-budget studies.

E5.justification: Both versions state that experiments are conducted five times and report averages. Neither introduces seed details, confidence intervals, error bars, significance tests, or another uncertainty-reporting procedure.

E6.justification: v2 adds extensive benchmark, detection, low-degree, and trigger-size results. New heterophilic tests report RIGBD ASRs of 0%, 3.3%, and 3.7% on Wisconsin, Cornell, and Texas. In the retained PubMed/DPGBA comparison, Table 2 changes RIGBD ASR/ACC from 0.01/84.32 to 0.03/84.56, although v2 Table 10 retains the earlier pair.

T1.justification: The graph assumptions, three theorems, concentration bound, complexity derivations, and Appendix D proofs remain substantively unchanged. The added low-degree and heterophily material is empirical rather than new theory.

C1.justification: The abstract, introduction’s contribution list, and conclusion retain the same claims about prediction variance, efficient poisoned-node identification, robust training despite missed nodes, and reduced attack success while maintaining clean accuracy. Broader experiments support these existing claims.

C2.justification: Appendix F discusses smaller prediction-variance separation on heterophilic graphs and interprets differences through prediction-confidence shifts. Appendix H.4 adds practical explanations of baseline weaknesses, especially ABL’s isolation-ratio dependence. Appendix R explicitly discusses training-stage defense and future inference-stage techniques.

D1.justification: v2 adds a code-access link in the abstract and Appendix Q, documents the all-neighbors-dropped fallback, and describes the added datasets’ features and labels. Hardware and validation-based hyperparameter tuning disclosures remain unchanged.

R1.justification: v2 adds references including Trojan Prompt Attacks and Xing et al.’s clean-label graph attack, while removing the introductory link-prediction citation. Appendices A.1 and H.4 sharpen positioning around attached triggers and dirty-label node-level attacks, but retain the central relationship to prior defenses.

P1.justification: The title changes, citations switch to author–year style, and acknowledgments, comparison discussion, reproducibility, and limitations sections are added. Existing appendices are renumbered around additions, while most main-text wording and the narrative sequence remain intact.

P2.justification: Table 2 expands from three to six dataset groups and is substantially compressed. Dataset, clean-accuracy, and detection tables expand, and new Tables 5, 9, and 12 display additional analyses. The ICLR template changes headers and typography throughout; existing figures are retained and repositioned.

improvement.justification: v2 substantially strengthens v1’s citation-network-only validation through broader graph domains and targeted tests of low-degree confounding, heterophily, and smaller triggers. These additions address important previously untested applicability conditions. Reporting defects temper the gain: Tables 2 and 10 disagree on some scores, and Appendix L retains an above-80% recall claim despite reporting 69.5% for Flickr/GTA. These limited inconsistencies do not outweigh the substantial improvement in empirical support.
